images.caption: Execution room of the Museum of Genocide Victims. Between 1944 and 1962, more than 1000 prisoners were executed in this room and later buried in mass graves outside Vilnius. Objects found in these mass graves are now on display within the glass cases located across the floor of the room.

images.caption:
This forbidding building, facing Gediminas Avenue in Vilnius, is the former KGB headquarter in Lithuania, where tens of thousands Lithuanians were interrogated and imprisoned in dark cellars, many also tortured and killed. 

Fittingly, this is now home to the Museum of Genocide Victims whith some of the old cells in the cellar open for visits. Entrance is from the other side of the building, in the quiet Aukų street.

images.caption: The facade of the former KGB building on Gedimino prospektas 40 in Vilnius has been inscribed with the names of Lithuanias killed while fighting for an independent country. Many of them were partisans who had first fought the Nazi German occupation but after the end of World War II switched to fight the Soviet occupation. Armed resistance in the Baltic actually continued for ten years after WWII, until the Soviet authorities managed to infiltrate the resistance movement and kill the leaders.

images.caption: The unassuming entrance to the Museum of Genocide Victims in the former KGB building in Aukų gatvė 2 in the heart of old town Vilnius, Lithuania. This museum is a stark reminder of the horrors of an authoritarian police state, but it also shows the bravery of the men and women who fought for the independence of Lithuania in the dark years after World War II.

images.caption:
Information about the Museum of Genocide Victims in old town Vilnius:

The museum is housed in the 19th century neo-classical mansion previously used as a court building. The main facade with a front entrance faces Gediminas Avenue. Throughout the Soviet era (1940 to 1941 and 1944 to 1991) the building was occupied by the Soviet repressive institutions such as the NKVD, NKGB, MGB, KBG while during the period 1941 to 1944, the Gestapo reigned in the building. Out of this building came the evil thoughts for the extermination of residents and persecution of the otherwise minded. The basement of the building served as a prison for the Nazis while the Soviets used it as a prison with an execution chamber inside. The stones of the plinth area of the edifice bear the names of the freedom fighters killed from 1944 to 1947. Apart from the museum visually displaying information on the Soviet occupation, the building houses the courts, the Genocide and Resistance Research Centre of Lithuania and the Lithuanian Special Archives where the former KGB archive documents are stored.
